newsitem.title: FRANCE: L'Aeropostale sees further 97 Europe cargo growth.
newsitem.headline: L'Aeropostale sees further 97 Europe cargo growth.

text.p: French airline L'Aeropostale said it was looking to continue its international development in 1997.
"We hope to do this through partnerships and contracts with airlines and postal utilities in Europe and beyond," L'Aeropostale's chief executive Martin Vial said.

L'Aeropostale currently operates one scheduled intra-European all-cargo service, between Paris and Cologne, on behalf of Global Delivery Express Worldwide (GDEW), a joint venture between express operator, TNT and several national post offices.
The airline's fleet comprises 21 aircraft -- 16 quick-change planes (14 737-300QCs and two 737-200QCs), plus one 737-300F, two 737-200Fs and two 727Fs.
It carries freight by night between France's major cities for the French post office and its express arm, Chronopost, TAT Express and Air France Europe.
By day, L'Aeropostale's fleet is used to transport passengers on behalf of the Air France group and Air Charter, on scheduled and charter services.
L'Aeropostale tabled 1996 net profits of 6.9 million francs compared to 7.2 million in 1995, from a turnover of 1.06 billion, up 5.3 percent on the previous year, the airline's figures showed.
Last year, L'Aeropostale handled 117,000 tonnes of freight, an increase of 10.8 percent on 1995, while passenger traffic was up 11 percent to 1,345,000 passengers.
The gap between the growth in traffic and turnover was explained by the preferential rates granted by L'Aeropostale to its customers in keeping with the objectives set for the airline, Vial added.

"L'Aeropostale's principal shareholders, Air France and the French post office (each with a 50 percent stake), are also its principal customers and provided the airline with 90 percent of its business in 1996," he said.
For 1997, L'Aeropostale was forecasting a two percent increase in turnover, with growth in freight traffic estimated at 1.6 percent and passenger traffic to rise by almost eight percent.

"1997 will also be a year of consolidation with the airline adapting itself to new operating conditions in the air transport sector in France and Europe in order to maintain a leading position," it said.
L'Aeropostale added that in operating 50 flights on a nightly basis, it was the second biggest air transporter of freight in Europe on short- and medium-haul routes, behind DHL .
